utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Harmon, are you ready to cross-examine Ms. Cenic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to have the same problem that Mr. Stewart had in terms of my asking you questions. You will have to delay, if you can, for just a few moments so the interpreters can catch up.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to get some dates in mind Mrs. Cenic. Specifically you testified you arrived in Vogosca approximately 15th of April. When did you leave Vogosca? Approximately what date?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could have been the beginning of July, and I'm not sure of the exact date unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I understood your testimony to be that from approximately the beginning part of May until the time you left, you slept and worked in the Park Hotel. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less so. At the beginning of May, we moved to the Park Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I understood that you didn't move very much from the Park Hotel because you considered it to be too dangerous.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My movements from the Park Hotel were to the house of Mr. Tintor, to his parents, who were old and who needed help. Also, to my parents' place where my daughter was staying in Ilijas. Whenever I could get a ride, I would go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you do that frequently?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As often as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you give me an estimate to the best of your recollection how many times from May until the time you left the municipality you travelled to those two locations?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first location, i.e. Mr. Tintor's house, was rather close so that it wasn't a problem to get there as far as the distance was concerned. And sometimes I would go there daily but, in any case, on several occasions every week. As far as my family in Ilijas is concerned, we are talking a greater distance here, but I would still go there at least twice a week. However, it all depended on the situation. I cannot talk about regular time intervals. It depended on whether I could get a ride and whether I could go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you were at the Park Hotel you worked in Mr. Tintor's office; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one might call it his office, although Ms. Cvijetic and I shared one room, one office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you aware or did you subsequently become aware that Mr. Tintor was a member of the SDS Main Board and a founding member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew this even before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, what was Mr. Tintor's views in respect of the Serb Radical Party in the positions and the philosophy of the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never discussed the Serb Radical Party with him. Therefore, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your evidence in the last two sessions, you said that you got along well with the people who worked in Mr. Tintor's office. You mentioned Mr. Koprivica, and then you said, "Except for Mr. Tintor, because relations with him were almost non-existent towards the end." Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at my statement, and I know what I said, I said that when I left and went to Pale and he also left without an intention to return to Vogosca, by then our relationship was almost non-existent, and if there was any relationship, it was really bad before he left as he was getting to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Mr. Tintor, in my view, was getting ready to leave us without saying a word to anybody, either to me or to Ms. Cvijetic or anybody for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he in fact just one day leave or were you informed by him that he was intending to leave and go to Pale and assume a different position?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became aware that he had decided not to return when I was in the Kikinda facility, when I came across him and when I saw that he was waiting to be received by Dr. Karadzic. And I simply realised that he had no intention of returning to Vogosca from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember when approximately that was?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the same time when I found myself in Pale, although I would return to Vogosca after him. Actually, I went once, and I also went to see my family, and I explained to my family that I would try and find any sort of accommodation for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you said that Mr. Tintor assumed the position as an advisor to the president. I'd like to show you an exhibit. And if the exhibits could be distributed. What you'll receive, Mrs. Cenic, is a set of two volumes of materials. They're tabbed on the side, and I'll refer you to a number, and then if you would direct your attention the specific number in the tab we'll talk about the exhibit I've referred you to. This first tab, Mrs. Cenic, is tab 40. If you turn to tab 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It needs a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 40, Your Honours, will be P1140. Sorry, Your Honours, P1139.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document, Mrs. Cenic, is a decision dated the 24th of August, 1992. It's a decision on the appointment of the Presidency's advisor, and it indicates that Jovan Tintor is appointed advisor to the Serb republic Presidency for the issues of accommodation and return of refugees, and it is type-signed by the president of the Republika Srpska Presidency, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. Was this the position, Mrs. Cenic, that Mr. Tintor assumed immediately after he left the municipality of Vogosca or was there another position that he may have assumed or do you know?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thank you for the opportunity for me to see this document. I claim that already in July Mr. Tintor discussed his future position as an advisor. I know for a fact that it was his wish to be the advisor for reconstruction or something to that effect, and he discussed that matter with Dr. Karadzic, and he negotiated that position with Dr. Karadzic. I know that because as I've already told you, he had spoken to Dr. Karadzic several times, and he voiced a few comments to that effect in front of me as well. I know that this was his wish. However, I can see in this document that he was appointed the advisor for refugees and the accommodation and return of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Cenic, you -- your testimony also was that -- that Mr. Tintor travelled frequently to Pale prior to his ultimate departure from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, may I just interrupt you. I take it that the witness looked at the English version of tab 40. I see tab 40 looks very much as a -- well, kind of a legal text dated the 29th of September 1992, whereas the English seems to be a decision on the appointment of the Presidency's advisor. I don't know whether you have a similar original.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have an original, Your Honour. Since I can't read the text, I'm trying to find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It goes for me from something like article or paragraph 16 until 26, but it has got nothing to do apparently --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If it's been placed in here by error, Your Honour, we will replace it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Registrar is so kind as to draw my attention to the fact that the English translation, last four digits ERN is 9388, whereas in the original it's 9288. It would be highly appreciated, Mr. Harmon, to have the materials checked. Although the Chamber will assist you but would not like to take over your task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll tend to that immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it's not the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you testified, Mrs. Cenic, that Mr. Tintor travelled frequently to Pale. He met the members of the presidency. He met Mr. Krajisnik. Were you aware that Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Tintor referred to each other as kum?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend their meetings, so I wouldn't know, but I know that there is a relationship between the families. One set of parents were godfather and godmother to the other set of parents or something to that effect. I never attended their meetings, and I really don't know how they addressed each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and let me show you a video, Mrs. Cenic. We're going to play it. This is from Prosecution Exhibit 529, Hanson tab 223, and you'll find that, Mrs. Cenic, in tab 47, I'm going to direct you to the English portion that you'll be seeing. You can hear it. If you turn to page 8 of the English portion. We're going to be playing a portion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I see no paging on the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring to the English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And since Mrs. Cenic can read English I was directing her to the English --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 8. Above the counter number, Mrs. Cenic, 0.26:22 we're going to be listening to a part of that film. So if you could pay attention to the monitor in front of you. If you would like to put on your headphones you can hear the interview in the original language.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Organisation of defence. We came to Zuc and we conquered that very important strategic point, and we connected to Pofalici. However, once I officially asked from Pofalici representatives to come for a discussion, they came few times and one time I said that they should come up. However, they didn't. They didn't accept that at the time. They didn't accept that plan. After that, I issued the order twice. I told them that they had to retreat so that we can make an action and go down to the city, because I was informed, I was present at a meeting in Vrace where Mr. Kukanjac was supposed to be present, too. I wasn't lucky to meet him that time, but I met our president, General Subotic, President Karadzic, President Krajisnik, Mico Stanisic, Momcilo Mandic. At that meeting we spoke about getting together to cut the city in two and, well, to enter the city using that bridge, the former fraternity and unity bridge."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, first of all, do you recognise the speaker in that video you just saw?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's Jovan Tintor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And to put the conversation in context, there's a reference to Pofalici and essentially an attack, an attempt to divide the city of Sarajevo. Do you recall that only the 14th of May through the 17th of May there was a large offensive action that was taken by the Bosnian Serbs directed toward the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tintor ever discuss with you his meeting with President Karadzic, President Krajisnik, Mico Stanisic, Momcilo Mandic, in an attempt to cut the city of Sarajevo in two?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember any conversations that you had with Mr. Tintor where he related to you the nature and substance of the conversations he had had with the Bosnian Serb leadership in Pale when he had returned from Pale to the Vogosca municipality?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Then we will turn to a different area, Mrs. Cenic. You said in your evidence that when you were working at the Park Hotel you were working with another woman who was Mr. Tintor's secretary, a woman by the name of Branka Cvijetic. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another portion of the interview that we have just seen with Mr. Tintor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It again, Your Honours, is P529, Hanson tab 223.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In English version, Mrs. Cenic, if you turn to tab 47, I will direct you to page 5. The interview that we will be -- the interview segment that we will be hearing will be this portion that starts at the top of the page at counter 0:12:53 and we'll hear down to the last paragraph, 0:15:53. So if we can play that portion of the interview.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Across Bascarsija, and it means that the secret is how the. I kept it as one of my biggest secrets and I didn't -- I asked for my associates not to reveal this secret, not to let it go public or to let it see the light of day till a certain moment. However, if you know a Djogo, then you know Djogo. Well, in this republic I would say for the others to know. "Well you, see when we received -- when we started arming people - that was just before the war - there were controls everywhere and nothing could pass through. Moreover, when I succeeded in getting one truck of an armament and ammunition to Mokro, I left it in front of the house of my family, and I went to the city to see how and in which way to transport those weapons. I met with Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, and she told me that they had searched her car the same day. What is more, they were so impertinent they took out everything from her purse, I mean her personal things. I took it as a serious warning that I should not try to get to Vogosca in that truck full of weapons and ammunition. However, I formed a wedding procession. I called on my most loyal people, and we put together 32 personal vehicles. We loaded them during the night, and the day after we decorated the cars with flowers and then the bride. I had a bride. She was my ex secretary, Ms. Branka, at the time, a girl from Serbia. She was the bride. And I was even shooting in the air while we were passing through Sarajevo as a wedding procession. I mean, I don't remember when I was happy or more satisfied when I -- because my trick worked. We passed through Sarajevo, and the police and all people, a lot of them applauded while we were passing and shooting, like, you know, a wedding procession. "And your trunks with a lot of ammunition and weapons. There were barricades. People thought it strange that Joja Tintor who was always there, and the leadership of the SDS, mostly seen at the press conferences, most of the journalists knew who you were but then again some people who came from the side didn't know who was that man sitting at the corner of the table. Barricades were set up and you were not there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, there's one major discord between the spoken and the written translation which I'd like to clarify. In writing it says that these cars, "We loaded them with weapon and ammunition during the night." "With weapon and ammunition" does not appear in the oral translation we just received. Could we verify whether this was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter doesn't remember whether she heard the words "weapons and ammunition." It may well have been the case but it is very difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand the difficulty of -- you can't ask the speakers to slow down a bit, isn't it. Mr. Stewart, could you please together with your team members pay attention to it whether they heard anything to the extent that they heard anything about loading with weapons and ammunition so we know what is the correct translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The -- I'm sorry, I had supposed that the interpreter's booth had got the document that they're giving us a different translation of, because when I -- when I started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were a few there were a few differences, for example, also at the end "and you were not there" where it reads "the holiday" -- "you were not at the Holiday Inn." So there are a few differences. I draw your attention to it not to, at this moment, to fully explore it but to find out especially until respect of this loading with weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But the only reason -- sorry, Your Honour, it's not a trivial point, it's -- we have the previous extract and just at the very beginning I got the impression - perhaps wrongly - I got the impression that the interpreter's booth must have got the same document we were looking at and reading that. If they don't, Your Honour, then we end up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They received the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it doesn't seen that the interpreters with their own responsibility here, if they, for example, would have heard, "you were not in the" -- "not there" instead of "in the Holiday Inn," of course I would expect them to translate what they hear, although assisted. Yes. Let's not spend -- the only thing I want to know is not to explore the whole of the procedure because I hardly ever heard any inconsistencies, but I noticed there were a few. One of them being of some importance and therefore I'd like to have this --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have a suggestion, Your Honour. This is not a very long tape. We can go to the counter at 0:13:31 and we can play and take a matter of minutes if the language assistants are listening in the original language.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That seems most satisfactory, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, let's go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are now, for the record, starting at counter 0:13:32, and if we could play through 0:15:28 or until the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As soon as we heard the loading, I think that's the major -- was the imagine are problem. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] When we started arming people that was just before the war. There were controls everywhere and nothing could pass through. Moreover, when I succeeded in getting one truck of armament and ammunition to Mokro, I left it in front of the house of my family, and I went to town to see how and in which way to transport those weapons. I met with Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, and she told me that they had searched her car the same day. They were so impertinent that they even took out everything from her purse, I mean her personal belongings. I took it as a serious warning that I should not try to get to Vogosca in that truck full of weapons and ammunition. However, I formed a wedding procession. I called on my most loyal people, and we put together 32 personal vehicles. We loaded them with weapons during the night, and the day after we decorated the cars with flowers and then the bride. I had a bride. She was my ex-secretary, Ms. Branka, at the time, a girl from Serbia. She was the bride."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have the weapons now but no ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, weapons; no ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be corrected on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So both the oral interpretation and the written translation have some right of existence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Cenic, as you can see from the film, Mr. Tintor's quite proud of that coup that he pulled before the war in arming the people of the Vogosca municipality. He also says that he had asked his associates not to reveal it. Did either Mr. Tintor or Ms. Cvijetic reveal it to you? Were you aware of this -- this feat that Mr. Tintor was very proud of?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had only heard bits and pieces about a wedding party, not the rest. But if I may add, Mr. Tintor had never been a hero, ever in his life, although he very much liked to think of himself as one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me then see if I understand your answer, pull it up. My question was: Were you aware of the provision of arms by Mr. Tintor through the means of this -- of a wedding party that is described in his interview with Risto Djogo?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, and I can clarify, yes, I had heard bits and pieces about that from Mr. Tintor. I didn't know the details then, and I don't know them now, because Mr. Tintor was given to boasting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you another excerpt from this very same video, Mrs. Cenic. I am again referring to tab 47 and it is P529, Hanson tab 223. I'd like to refer you to page 9 in the English. At the bottom of the page Mrs. Cenic, counter number 0:31:13. And if we could play that portion of the interview with Mr. Tintor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] So it was then that you took over the Pretis factory which is a very important military industry --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The problem we're having here is that although -- of course, the interpretation booth are interpreting. If Mr. -- sorry, Mr. Harmon does not give the page references in the Serbian version, Mr. Krajisnik is unable to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He can follow the spoken text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I also -- I gave the counter number which is in the B/C/S version. There's a counter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not in mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't mind, Your Honour, if an explanation is given which then does enable Mr. Krajisnik to follow then I'll -- I can just drop out. But I'm registering that at the moment so far he has found difficulty in following.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try, Mr. Harmon, to accommodate Mr. Krajisnik. At the same time, of course, the words spoken --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The position is and Your Honour will have sympathy with this, Mr. Krajisnik wishes to both listen and follow the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll try to do our utmost best. Mr. Harmon, you were pointing us at page 9, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 9, 0:31:13, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just -- page 9. Yes. I was trying to fine the commercial, but -- yes. I think we find it on the page, last three digits 240, where I found at the bottom both the name of, I take it, wrongly spelled, Kukanjac, the Pretis, and the Tas. Yes. It should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It may be at the bottom of 241, Your Honour. If you go to 24 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where would you start on page 9, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would start at page 9, starting Mr. Djogo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, he appears twice. He appears twice on that page. On the bottom or on the middle?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The bottom of the middle, that's page -- last two digits, 41. I take it approximately a little bit below the middle of the page, Mr. Krajisnik. Yes. Let's -- you found it? Yes. Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] So it was then that you took over the factory Pretis, which is a very important part of military industry. Let's go back, further back to the time before the war. Even before the war you've already seen the NATO base in Zurich. How did you get there and what were you doing there? T: "Well, you see although we received a large amount of arms from our civilian protection from the former Yugoslav People's Army and some things we took by force some things we received and some things we got on this and that way, we had to be provided through our people that were working abroad. They made it possible for me to enter the NATO base in Zurich and there we took, well, pretty solid amount of arms and --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't see the last part of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're not having much luck, Your Honour, today. For the last part of the text we'll have to go back and -- in the middle of this video and play it again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The transcript reads "to transport it to our republic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- well, at least the word "republic" appears in the original. If there is any problem, Mr. Stewart, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me -- and then Mrs. Cenic, I want to refer you to tab 25 as well.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to show you two documents, tabs 25 and 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tab 25 already has a number, Your Honour. It's P51 is. This has been exhibited many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, if you would -- let me explain what this document is. This document is a document that is dated the -- there's a cover letter of the 20th of March, 1992. It's a military secret. It is directed to the General Staff of the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia by commander General Colonel Milutin Kukanjac, and this document, if you would turn to the English, page 6 of this document. In this document General Kukanjac has reported to his superiors that on the volunteer units in the zone in the 2nd Military District and in sub-part (b) of his report under number 5 he says that the total number of volunteers is just 69.198 people. And if you go down to (f), he reports that the JNA has distributed 51.900 pieces of armament (75 per cent) and SDS 17.298 pieces. Now, this document needs to be read in conjunction with the document that you'll find in tab 26, which is Prosecution Exhibit P101. This document, an attachment to General Kukanjac's report, lists 75 locations, as you'll see, and the numbers are the number of men in -- at those locations. If you turn -- if you look at item 5, Vogosca, it refers to 1.500, and if you go to the total, the total is 69.198. So the number of arms that were distributed to the men is -- this document correlates with the previous document of General Kukanjac's report. We've heard, Mrs. Cenic, from the interview with Mr. Tintor where he said he received arms from the JNA before the war started, General Kukanjac reporting that both the SDS and the JNA were providing arms to volunteers, and 1.400 arms being distributed to volunteers in the Vogosca municipality. Were you aware of that level of organisation and arming of the Bosnian Serb people in the Vogosca municipality prior to the start of the war?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does this surprise you, Mrs. Cenic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that it surprises me. It shocks me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why so?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was under a different impression. My experience of it all is completely different. This is really the first time that I see how well-armed the Serbs were and that there was such large numbers of people involved. This is a large amount of people. I didn't see as many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me -- it appears then, doesn't it, Mrs. Cenic, that the Serb people of the Vogosca municipality were preparing well in advance of the start of the conflict to arm themselves?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I didn't know that they were this well prepared. They didn't seem well prepared to me at all. Or prepared at all, for that matter. This is an honest reply I'm giving you, and I am here solely for the truth, nothing else. I am indeed shocked that -- even too mild a statement for what I feel. I am shocked by the sheer numbers. If the document indeed refers to Vogosca in mentioning 1.500 people, I must say I don't remember seeing as many people at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me take you back to tab 25, Mrs. Cenic, which is General Kukanjac's report, and again if I can refer you, please, to sub-part 5 of his report. Sub-part (f).

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] (f).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Dealing with the distribution in weapons. And in this report of General Kukanjac, he says that the SDS distributed 17.298 pieces. What's your reaction to that, Mrs. Cenic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wonder where these large numbers of SDS members were. If this figure -- or, rather, corresponds to the number of members or if as many pieces of weaponry were intended for as many SDS members, then I wonder where these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question to you, Mrs. Cenic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could there be -- Mr. Harmon, could there be any confusion? Ms. Cenic, when you gave your last answer where you said you wondered where these people were, what area or what territory did you have in mind? Did you want to say to us that you wondered whether there were so many SDS members in Vogosca, or were you saying that you wonder that there were so many SDS members in the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or were you telling us that you wondered whether so many people were in the municipalities listed on this list in tab 26, which are 75.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take the answer to your question in the following order: First of all, let's go back to the 1.500 volunteers from Vogosca who I had never seen there. I had never seen so many numbers of people in the streets armed, whether they be JNA members, volunteers, or whoever. That's number one. Number two, based on this letter or report by General Kukanjac that so many weapons were distributed to SDS members drives me to ask myself where these people were. I'm simply reasoning logically the war could have been won with such large quantities of weapons had as many weapons been distributed to members of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what the text says. The text says that they were distributed -- General Kukanjac was reporting that both the SDS and the JNA were providing arms to volunteers, not necessarily SDS members but distributed in the amount as Mr. Harmon quoted by JNA or by SDS, the SDS distributing some -- a little bit over 17.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- suggest this? That sometimes in the wish to speed things along, with respect, we go too quickly, and the heart of some of what appears to be confusion here lies, I suggest, at page 19, line 6 and 7, because in quickly referring this witness to sub-part (f) in the report and simply referring to 17.298 pieces, what seems to have happened is we glossed over the fact that the area being referred to in that bit of the report is different from what was previously being considered in relation to the 1.500 weapons. And if that is borne in mind, my submission is we begin to see how these last few answers have got tangled up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm being a little cryptic, Your Honour, because I'm not giving evidence and the witness is here. But I'm trying to just draw attention to where the difficulty lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Cenic, the 1.500, that's clear. You say, "I didn't see 1.500 armed men in Vogosca," so that's a clear answer. Then you also said, "I wondered where these 17.000 would be." Well, 17.000 would be men having been armed. From what I understand, Mr. Harmon, it's at least the position in this report somewhere --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in these 75 municipalities. And when you said, "I wonder where they were," could you not imagine 17.000 Serbs having been armed in 75 municipalities? Is that what you were wondering or were you under the impression that the 17.000 would be in Vogosca or near Vogosca or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, going back to page 6, items 5 (f) it reads that the JNA distributed 51.900 and the SDS 17.298. I apologise. This is the first time I see this. The question was put to me rather quickly, and I had time to chance at item (f). Now, I have no idea about this, but the SDS never appeared to me to be a party that was well off or affluent. That was why I was wondering at this figure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is, we submit, that one can't really pick out subparagraph (f) here without looking at least at subparagraph (e) and then probably at subparagraph (a), because this is all referring to an area, to start with, at the beginning of this section which is identified on a map, and then subparagraph (e) is referring to a number of listed municipalities. So before -- and this is where we got to, really. Before the witness could fairly be asked to comment on the figure in subparagraph (f), we did need to be as clear as possible to what that figure is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I make a submission as well, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Subparagraph E deals with a different military district. It deals with the 4th Military District which then lists the municipalities within the 4th Military District. It has no relationship to the volunteers in the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- let's try to keep things simple. Ms. Cenic, you had any knowledge or no knowledge about distribution of arms by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said you wondered where they were, I now understand that you were not aware that the SDS would even have the means to provide arms in such quantities. Is that a correct understanding of your last answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That sufficiently clarifies the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It sufficiently clarifies the matter at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I must make a submission, Your Honour. Mr. Harmon's comment, of course he's trying to help us all to unravel this as well, but he draws attention to the fact the 2nd Military District is different from the 4th Military District but, Your Honour, it's nevertheless mentioned specifically. Your Honour, it is not sufficiently clear in my submission where we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart. I eliminated the whole of what districts whatsoever. The witness clearly testified, and I was not putting this in her mouth but it was her last answer, that she was surprised and wondered that the SDS would be well off enough to provide these arms, and that is a clear answer. And where 2nd Military District and whatever else, I did not understand the witness to -- to further specify that, but if her answer would not be true in general and would be limited to only the 2nd or the 4th Military District, she'll tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, the question Your Honour put at line 18 of page 22, given the confusion that there had plainly been over the previous few minutes is not sufficiently clear because it needs to be made clear whether Your Honour was asking about the SDS in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina or some big area or some small area, because such is the ambiguity and uncertainty about what we were dealing with that one cannot simply take that question and answer at face value without it being absolutely plain that the witness understands exactly what area is being spoken about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Cenic, when you said more or less that you were surprised that the SDS would have been well enough -- well off to distribute those arms. Did you speak in general about SDS in Bosnia-Herzegovina or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have any specific area or part of the country in mind. The figure as such to me seemed rather high, and I didn't know just as I don't know now as I'm looking at this piece of paper that the SDS could have secured such large amounts regardless of who the weapons were intended for or which areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, aside from your reservations about whether the SDS was affluent enough to have secured 17.298 weapons, are you surprised that they were distributing weapons in the time prior to the start of the war?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am surprised. I'm surprised by the quantity. I did see weapons. Of course I did, because the security guards for Dr. Karadzic and others carried weapons. Furthermore, Mr. Tintor, as you already know, traded in weapons. He had a weapons shop before the war. It was registered to sell weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mrs. Cenic. I move to another subject if the Court has no questions. Mrs. Cenic, you testify -- I want to talk about the takeover the municipality building, and your testimony was that the municipality building was empty and that Mr. Tintor, Koprivica, and others, entered the building and essentially tried to organise the work of the municipality. Is the municipality building the same as the Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the municipality building in Vogosca where the management of the municipality is located, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were you present when Mr. Tintor and others entered that building, or did you just hear about it from Mr. Tintor and others?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't there, and I stated that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next exhibit, which is found at tab 35. This needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1140, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a -- an article from Nas Glas it's dated 13th of July 1992. The headline is "Vogosca Has Perspective" and it's an interview with Rajko Koprivica. And I'd like to direct your attention -- I'll just read part it. I'm going to ask you your comments. "On the" -- and I'm starting at the top of the article, Mrs. Cenic. "On the occasion of the 3-month existence of Vogosca Serbian municipality, journalists in Nas Glas and the Serbian radio talked with Rajko Koprivica, the President of the Executive Board. Mr. President, could you summarise events in Vogosca during the past three months?" The answer: "Despite the fact that it's been three months, the Serbian municipality of Vogosca started functioning only since and month and a half ago. During the period prior to that, it existed formally, because we thought that we would manage to reach a peaceful agreement with the opposing side on the division of power based on the principle of four local communes where the Muslim people are the majority in four of which the Serbian people are the majority. This proposal surprised them and they categorically rejected it. Right before the war there was a period of calm in which they got into the assembly and put pressure on Serbian deputies with the help of the left bloc. Thinking that we would lose power without a single bullet fired, we set up a Crisis Staff and one morning stormed the Assembly building and took control of. When they saw that, they asked for negotiations but not on the principle of four local communes but on the principle of majority population." Now, this article is interesting. It asserts -- Mr. Koprivica asserts that there was a Crisis Staff that was set up and that the Crisis Staff was set up at least prior to the building being stormed. Is there any reason you have to dispute that assertion?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can see, the date is 13 July, and the article speaks about three months, which corresponds to the period that I have spoken about. I know and I've said that, that they entered the municipality, that there was nobody there, and that there was no fighting. That's one thing that I know. And the second thing I know is the fact that there was a body and that even before that, as I've already stated, they would meet in Mr. Koprivica's house from time to time for consultations, that there was a Crisis Staff and then the Presidency of the municipality I know as well. I know nothing about any negotiations because I never participated in any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, that was going to be my next question, because Mr. Koprivica asserts in this article that after the municipal building -- the Assembly building was stormed that the Muslims wanted to engage in negotiations, and my question is: What did you hear about that? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details of that. I don't know how the negotiations developed. I really don't know. I wasn't present. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Prior to the start of the war in the Vogosca municipality or prior to the takeover - I'm sorry - of the Assembly building that we've just been talking about, had you heard Mr. Kopravica or Mr. Tintor saying things to the effect that "We can't live with the Muslims any longer"?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I don't remember a conversation to that effect with any one of them. Especially I don't remember Mr. Kopravica ever saying that. Mr. Tintor would sometimes be rather radical in his statements, but Mr. Kopravica never uttered any word to that effect. I haven't heard him say anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, following the takeover of the municipality building, were you aware, Mrs. Cenic, that Bosnian Muslim civilians were arrested and detained in the Vogosca municipality?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of just one prison, if I can call it that, which was near the Sonja restaurant. I believe that there were one or two rooms there and since I never went there, I never entered those premises, I can't give you the surface of those rooms. I know that this was a very small house, a very small building across the road from the restaurant itself. I don't know of anything else of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you become aware of the prison at Sonja's restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the date with any degree of certainty. I believe that this was during the time when we were at the Park Hotel, and I believe that I heard it from a policeman. The only policeman that I never spoke to. His name is Brane Vlaco. I remember his name because he was on the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear then or subsequently, up to the present time, that the restaurant at Sonja's house was a location where Muslim women were held against their will and raped?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Later on when I came to Vogosca with that journalist, that restaurant was the place where somebody was accommodated, somebody whose name I can't remember. I remember what he looked like. He was killed later on. But at the same time, the restaurant was patroned by some officers of the peace corps. So I really can't confirm. I can't remember that any such thing happened in this restaurant. When I arrived once or two times, when I went to that restaurant I really didn't see any such thing. I didn't see anything there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, if you would kindly turn to tab 2. This is a picture we're familiar with in this court. It's Prosecution Exhibit [inaudible]. This is a house that's known as Planja's house, and it gives an address. The Court has heard considerable evidence about that house being a prison and indeed the -- there is a document that the Court has seen also which is Prosecution Exhibit 1097 in which on the 7th of July the Vogosca municipality secretariat for town planning essentially allocated this house as a prison to be used by the Ministry of Justice. First off, have you ever seen this house? Are you familiar with this house? I know the address is indicated on the right -- lower right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the house, but I personally can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have passed this house. I'm not excluding the possibility. But I can't say anything else. If I said anything else it would be pure speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you can't help us with this house being used as a prison in Vogosca municipality in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Then let me turn your attention to another part of your evidence. You testified that -- and this is found at LiveNote pages 22 and 23 on day 248, you were asked if there were any type of organised unit of soldiers, and your answer was: "At the time, during the first weeks of confusion that prevailed, there were no organised units." And you went on to say that you didn't see any units of the former JNA present, but on one occasion you had seen Mr. Tintor in the presence of 50 men dressed in various types of clothes and armed. Now, other than seeing that one particular group of people, did you see any other groups of soldiers in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not soldiers. There was the police and there was this group of people that subsequent organised themselves into some units. I didn't see any other troops. I did not see any other army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn next, Mrs. Cenic, to tab 48. This is Prosecution Exhibit P601. This is the -- this is a text of an intercepted telephone communication on the 6th of April between Danilo Veselinovic and Jovan Tintor, and it's not a long text. If you could just cast your eye on it quickly. I'm going to just direct your attention to a part of it that's on page 2. Why don't you cast your eye on the whole text, Mrs. Cenic, very quickly. Let me know what you at least --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Take a look at the whole intercept if you would.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All the pages?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For your information, Mrs. Cenic, as well, I should have told you there is a B/C/S version of the intercept behind the English version, if it's easier for you.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Veselinovic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic was also a member of the Main Board of the SDS. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in this conversation, Mrs. Cenic, if you turn to page 2 of the English version, line 29, Mr. Tintor says: "Well, we have that section completely under control, the army from my area." So on April the 6th, 1992, in this conversation at least, Mr. Tintor is referring to an army.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me just a few sentences. First of all, Jovan Tintor organised through the entire street the so-called Old Reljevo street some sort of guards of -- a guards' duty, because a lot of the population there had lost many members of their families during the Second World War. Mr. Vlado Tintor also lost some members of his family. This is the only army, if he's referring to anything as an army, that I saw in my whole life. Those were there. Those were men who resided in those houses and nothing else. And I know that. As for any other army that Mr. Tintor mentions in here, I've never heard or seen any such thing. And if you allow me just a brief comment, Mr. Tintor liked to brag a lot and exaggerate a lot. I repeat, this is the only thing I saw. I never saw anything else there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, Mrs. Cenic, to tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This needs a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 4, Your Honour will be P1141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, on my list tab 4 is an -- P529, tab 220.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have a new list, Your Honour I'm sorry -- I've been provided with a new list. So tab 4, Your Honour, does have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1141, Your Honours, would be available then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is P529, tab 220. This document, for the record, is an entitled Recapitulation of "Counter-transactions of Crisis Staff Cashier's Office from 1 May to 31 May 1992." Under sub-part 1 it indicates incoming payments, and it gives a sum, and the first item of incoming payments is aid SRBiH, 5 million dinars. And if you go down to outgoing statements from the Crisis Staff, which is subparagraph 2 and if you go to the penultimate figure in that column, you see that 14.215.000 dinars was paid out by the Crisis Staff for soldiers' daily allowance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this document, Mrs. Cenic, suggests that during the month of May there was -- there were considerable monies paid out to soldiers on behalf of the Crisis Staff. May I invite your comments on that, please?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I really don't know who Radovan Bilic is. Was that the gentleman who -- whom I knew as Raso or maybe somebody else? I really don't know. Second of all, as for the outgoing statements, I really don't know what to say. I don't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, again, I want to return, Mrs. Cenic, to the topic that we are discussing, and that is that there were no organised units in the municipality in the early part of the conflict. You'd mentioned Boro Radic, and in your evidence I recall you mentioned that Boro Radic was a tough guy. He had approximately 12 people around him. They had pistols. They're more the equivalent of a street gang than an army. And I'd like to direct your attention to tab 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing so, Mr. Harmon, could you or could the Defence assist me? Approximately the exchange rate at that time, what would be a million dinars? Well, I take it, it was always -- it was always converted in Deutschmarks, but -- or could the witness tell us? Do anyone know? I mean, 14 million.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sounds like a lot, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sounds a lot but -- DEFENCE COUNSEL: I'm afraid nobody including Mr. Krajisnik is able to produce that off-the-cuff, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to inform the Chamber, whoever knows first, to inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a competition between us then, Your Honour. We'll see what we can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you draw the attention of the witness to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention -- first of all, I want to draw your attention to a number of documents that in respect of Mr. Radic's unit. If we take a look at tab 36, it does need a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1141, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document, Mrs. Cenic, that appears to be a list of 22 people, which you'll see. It is -- it starts at -- it's identified as the special detachment at the top. The first person involved is Boro Borislav Radic who is identified as the commander. And then at the bottom it is written the signature Radic Borislav. So this appears -- and I'm sorry there also appears to be a date of May the 25th, 1992. So this unit appears to be a -- at least according to this item, a formal unit commanded by Mr. Radic numbering 22 men. What I'd like to do is turn your attention to tab 29, and then I'm going to ask you some questions. 29 also needs a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Let me just take a look at -- before I say that, let my double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It has a number, it's P529, tab 213. I'm sorry, 309.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic -- that's not the exhibit. I'm sorry. Tab 39. Tab 39 does need an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is -- this is also a document dated the 27th of June, 1992. It is -- at the top it says Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbian municipality of Vogosca War Commission. The subject of this is a request for issuing the vehicle, and it is essentially a request by the applicant, whose name is Ljubomir Tosovic, for a Golf vehicle, and identifies Mr. Tosovic as being part of the special unit of Boro Radic. So it appears that unit that Mr. Radic was a -- was a special unit, though, part of the armed formations that were in the Vogosca municipality, and they appear to be making requests to the War Commission, which is essentially the local government organisation. May I invite your comments on this document?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you my comments on every single document. Let me start with the first document first. The list of people that I can see here, I knew most of them, and the date is 25th of May. In my testimony, I've already said that at that time, i.e., when the line-up of these people took place, they actually became a unit. At that time, Boro Radic didn't play any role, save the one that I mentioned. I can also give you some names of people. For example, number 17, Zeljko Djuricic Kelja, whom I know well; Predrag Zarkovic Bozur, Sasa Vejin, Ljubomir Tosovic Suber, Slavisa Savic Sava, Radomir Prodanovic Gaga Slavisa Vukovic [as interpreted] Sava, Branislav Josipovic Josa, Sale Sasa Ivanovic. All those were lads or at least some of them. For example, under 17, Zeljko Djuricic Kelja, and Radomir Prodanovic Gaga, who also slept in the Park Hotel next to my room or across the hallway from my room. Some of the others either stayed in their houses. A lot of them are no longer amongst the living. For example, Predrag Zarkovic Bozur is no longer living. A few others are not alive either. Later on, as I've already told you, tensions between Boro Radic and Jovan Tintor came to a head, and the issue at stake was control, influence, and the underlying issue's always power, of course. I'm not excluding the possibility that these men were incorporated into some units. Boro Radic's unit. As for the request to issue a Golf vehicle, I had to laugh when this man is called a member of a special unit because whoever knew Tosovic would know that he looked more like a child than a special. And if I can provide another comment. In this wretched war that is behind us, every single person liked to call themself special, although they didn't look anything like specials. This would be my comment. This is what I know. Most of these men are no longer alive. When I departed, I don't know what -- what happened to that so-called unit. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me direct your attention, Mrs. Cenic, to tab 37. This needs a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: P1143, Mrs. Cenic is a document from the army of Republika Srpska Vogosca brigade command dated the 30th of December, 1992, and it's an order. And if you look at sub-part 1, under around, it says the Boro Radic Intervention Platoon of the Brigade commanded by Slavica Vukovic is hereby disbanded, and then it goes on it list a number of people in this. So if you do as I have done, Mrs. Cenic, I won't ask you to do the same exercise, but if you do a comparison of the names in the document that's in tab 36, the special detachment which is dated the 25th of May and you do a comparison of the names in the document in tab 37, you will find, for example, that many of the names are the same names. For example, I'll quickly identify them. At tab 37 you'll find in the first company, you'll find four names. Branislav Josipovic, Ljubomir Tosovic, Zivorad Markovic, and Nebojsa Trifkovic, as being in the same group of people as in the exhibit that's found in tab 36. If you go to the 2nd Company, you'll find item number 4, Boro Jovicic appears on the other list as well. If you go to the last list of names in the English version, which is the brigade's Reconnaissance Platoon, you'll find that numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4 also appear on the first list. So it appears, Mrs. Cenic, that the group of Radic special detachment soldiers identified on the 25th of May appear to have been incorporated into the Vogosca brigade itself and ultimately was disbanded on the -- by order on the 30th of September, 1992. So it appears that these people became incorporated into the -- into the army. My -- my question to you, Mrs. Cenic, is: What was your degree of awareness that Mr. Radic's group of soldiers was responsive to the Crisis Staff, to the command of the Bosnian Serb army? Are you in a position to assist us on that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can only say what I've been saying in the past couple of days, that later on these so-called units were placed under army command, because there was this military organisation. I said so explicitly. I believe I even mentioned the name of the major who I thought was commander of the entire region. I know that after Boro Radic was killed his, or, rather, the unit was named after him. I see these documents for the first time. Boro Radic himself was not answerable or accountable to either the Crisis Staff or the Presidency or the commission of Vogosca. As I said, I'm repeating, there was always this tension or even competitiveness, I'd say, between Tintor and Radic. In trying to think back about those events so many years later, I might even remember some more information, but I can't realty moment. I know the name of Miladen Trifunovic, and I remember quite a few of these names because at the time of this first grouping or the line-up, I don't know which -- how I called it, quite a few of the people mentioned here were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, did you know Boro Radic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were his duties in respect of the Muslims in the Vogosca community?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to tell you really. He was quite a difficult man to talk to. He was barely literate. Our conversations boiled down to simple sentences. We didn't go into any political, social, or - God forbid - cultural discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him express any anti-Muslim views, anti-Croat views, extremists' views of any kind?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't talk about that, believe me. I only know that his first or second wife was Muslim, if I remember. I believe he was married twice. One of his wives was Muslim or a Bosniak. I am certain that the two of us didn't have any other conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me then change the topic slightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, you are aware of the limited time you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am aware, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I have noticed that even we'll have to finish -- we can't finish at 7.00. We have even to finish a little bit earlier than that. So now we have -- it's clear from the answers of this witness that she had not detailed knowledge of many things that were described in written documents, so I wonder how important it would be to pursue this matter any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On this particular matter I've ended my examination, Your Honour. I'm just -- I was informed yesterday that I had three hours. I'm just interested to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think I said to stay well within three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I intend to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When will we take the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break with the -- we'll have to stop not later than quarter to seven, unfortunately, due to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we have one break a little bit longer than usual, but I need the -- I need the approval of the interpreters and the technicians, which would mean we would stop in approximately five minutes from now, and then to resume at 20 minutes past five and then to go on. And that of course, then, on from 20 minutes past five, Mr. Harmon it would not be all your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I'll finish within the time. The Court doesn't have to worry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm trying to bring down the average that the Court referred to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes the proof of the pudding is in the eating.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just direct your attention next, Mrs. Cenic, to tab 3.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes this is Prosecution Exhibit 1091. This is a transcript of a film that was a ceremony, and it was held on, if I recall, the 15th of May, 1992, in which Mr. Seselj anointed a number of new Chetnik vojvodas. Let me direct your attention to page 2 of this document, the English version. The counter number 00:34:36. And you'll see a number of Chetnik -- a number of individuals were given the rank of Chetnik vojvoda, one of whom, the third line from the bottom, was man by the name of Jovo Ostojic. Did you know Jovo Ostojic? Were you acquainted with him? Did you run into him when you were in the Vogosca municipality, Ms. Cenic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't remember, no. I'm trying to remember the name. Did the gentleman have a nickname of any sort? Because we knew each other by nicknames rather than by anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does the nickname Cica ring a bell? If you look at the text on page 2 and you see his name, you'll see in front of it -- it could well be --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- the previous person as well. So I don't see a nickname. You mentioned in your evidence yesterday that there were paramilitary members that you observed who were quite frightening. They wore, I think, skull insignias and various sorts of insignia that would frighten the people. Where did you see those paramilitaries, Mrs. Cenic? Did you see those people in the Vogosca municipality?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, as far as I remember, they came on two occasions, but none of the names mentioned here. Rather, it was Vaske Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this the appropriate time? I have to go into two other exhibits very quickly, but I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The two other exhibits we'll do it still in the time available on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. If that case if you take a look, please, at tab 15. This needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 15, Your Honours, will be P1144.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And we're going to be looking at that document as well in conjunction with the document that's found at tab 16, Mrs. Cenic. The document at tab 16 has a number. It's P762, tab 9. Let's start with the first document at tab 15. This is a document from the Vogosca Serbian municipality Executive Board. It is dated the 28th of July, 1992, and it's to the War Commission, and the subject is a remuneration for volunteers, and it indicates that -- and I'll read the text: "Volunteers engaged under the command of Jovo Ostojic, approval has been given in principle by representatives of Vogosca municipality that remuneration for the month of July be 300 Deutschmarks based on the exchange rate of 150 dinars for one Deutschmark."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Deal with the first, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm just going to say we have solved the previous problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "We would like you to -- we would like to ask you to make the appropriate decision in order to regulate this issue legally, formally," and it's signed by the president Rajko Kopravica. And if we turn then to tab -- the next tab, 16. This is a document that's in connection with the previous document. It's from the Serbian municipality of Vogosca, wartime commission, dated the 30th of July, 1992. And I'll just read this document: "Pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, number 01-33/92 of 10 June 1992, the wartime commission of the Serbian municipality of Vogosca reviewed at its session held on the 29th of July, 1992, a request submitted by the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly for a decision to be made on paying volunteers under Jovo Ostojic's command. The wartime commission adopted the follow conclusion: "1. In light of the military and political situation, the wartime commission believes that the soldiers of the Sosa detachment under Jovo Ostojic's command are indispensable for the defence of the Serbian municipality of Vogosca and that the necessary funds must be found to pay them. "2. In light of this assessment we have no objections to the manner, extent, and time of payment which the Executive Committee shall decide upon." It says "For the wartime commission." I would just first like to ask you, Ms. Cenic, if you could turn to the original page in the B/C/S at the lower right-hand portion there are two signatures. Can you identify those two signatures for us?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, paramilitary formations, when you were in the Vogosca municipality, Mrs. Cenic, did you see paramilitary formations that -- of individuals who dressed in what we have -- what's been referred to as Chetnik garb?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only paramilitary detachment or group that I saw was the one I already mentioned, and I said where they came from. As for the Susa detachment here, I don't know about it. I can see by the date that it's late July. I don't know. Jovo Ostojic, his first and last name really don't match up with any of the faces I knew there. Perhaps the gentleman had a nickname that I knew him by. At any rate, I find his name unfamiliar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me return to the man you named. Was it Vaske Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he came to Vogosca twice with his group of men. He went to the Park Hotel. There were no incidents related. I know him from Ilijas. Among other things, when Mr. Kent arrived who wanted to see everything, I showed him what this part of war folklore was like, and I apologise for this rather rough coinage, but I wanted him to see the people, to get to know them, and to film them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was Mr. Vidovic doing at the Park Hotel, from your observations?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He arrived. He saw where we were located at the time. He sat there for a while and then left. One of the girls, I believe there were two of them -- I believe he even brought his daughter along. There was there was never girl there to came asking for cough syrup or something of the sort. They were asking about some other medicines as well. That was this particular event which had to do with Vogosca. And I received a gift from him which was a crocheting piece of work or tapestry or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was Mr. Vidovic there alone or was he with members of his armed formation?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several people with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were they -- did they appear to be members of his same armed formation?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were with him, so that means ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, I may have some additional questions, but I'm conscious of the time. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I did some of calculations. 14 million at the level of 300 Deutschmarks a month at an exchange rate of 150 dinars for one Deutschmark brings us to, if paid equally, if paid on the same level to some 300 soldiers. We will adjourn until 20 minutes past five. I said earlier that I needed the consent of the interpreters. Do I have it? Yes. And then we'll stop at a quarter to seven. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me begin by just informing the Court that the document in tab 40, the B/C/S has now been replaced with the proper B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, let me begin by where we ended, because the text of the transcript had an incomplete answer, and I need to get your complete answer. You were -- I was asking you the question whether Mr. Vidovic was alone or was he with members of his armed formation. Your answer was: "There were several people with him." The next question I asked you was: "Did they appear to be members of your same armed formation." And your answer as it appears on the transcript, "They were with him, so that means," and then there are some ellipses. Could you complete your answer?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were there, yes, as part of his unit or group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do I understand that you saw him only on one occasion at the Park Hotel or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I saw him on two occasions, as far as I remember, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Again on the second occasion was he with members of his unit?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, was he merely having a drink at the Park Hotel or was he conducting some form of business insofar as you could see?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, they had no special business to conduct there. On both these occasions, as I said -- or, rather, on one of these occasions there was this girl asking for medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. We've exhausted that topic, Mrs. Cenic. I'm going to turn to another part of your evidence from yesterday. Yesterday, you testified that during the time that you were in Vogosca you were unaware of any instructions given by anybody in Pale to people in Vogosca in relation to matters in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That testimony, Your Honours, is found at page 41, lines 5 through 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And let me first of all begin by showing you some exhibits. If we could start at tab 8. This has -- 8 is Exhibit number P529, tab 322. Mrs. Cenic, this is the conclusion. It bears the date of 17th of May, 1992, in the lower left-hand corner but it is from the SSOV Serb Crisis Staff meeting that was held on the 16th of May, 1992. And I direct your attention to item number 1. It says: "An order is being issued for the takeover the army barracks at Semizovac. It is being placed under the command of the SSOV Crisis Staff, which is under the sole command of the Serb republic of BH."
