Now, that, Mrs. Cenic, indicates that the Crisis Staff was in a subordinate relationship and under a command relationship from the Serb republic of BH. And you have given us your early -- your earlier evidence at that Mr. Kopravica, Mr. Tintor, other people who held positions of power were going to Pale to meet with members of the leadership, and including Mr. Krajisnik, including Mr. Karadzic. Do you -- are you aware of those individuals receiving orders, any kind of orders from the people at the republic level?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the second item in this, and I'm going to ask you to comment on it. In part 2 of this conclusion it says: "From the cleansing of Svrake and other territories, one more man is to be secured apart from M. Borovcanin. The territory of Semizovac is to be ociscen in the -- in case there was shooting by terrorists and those trying to do provocations." First of all, do you know who M. Borovcanin is?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in Svrake to the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to item number 5. Item number 5 says: "Muslim and Croat staff at the Vogosca medical centre is to be put on hold." Do you know, Mrs. Cenic, what happened to the Muslim and Croat staff at the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there any discrimination against Muslim or Croat employees in public enterprises in the Vogosca municipality while you were there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't enter the premises and wasn't staff member of the companies or, rather, employee of the companies in Vogosca. There were only a few businesses that were active.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you hear of any reports while you were there, Mrs. Cenic, that Muslim or Croat employees lost their jobs after the takeover of the Municipal Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality had mixed staff, and the only logical inference I could make was that they had all been dismissed or had lost their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you finally to turn your attention to item number 7. It says: "The proper leaders of the military are obliged to submit daily reports on the situation in the brigade." Can you tell us what brigade Mr. Jovanovic was referring to?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know this gentleman, Rajko Jovanovic, and I can only assume that this has to do with this newly established brigade or group that I had described which had been -- or which, rather, was later on divided into some units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you can't enlighten us further on this brigade in Vogosca as of the 16th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, again focusing on your evidence that there were -- you were unaware of any instructions being received from Pale to Vogosca in respect of the events that were taking place in Pale, let me turn your attention to tab 33. This is previously exhibited document. It's found at P529, tab 120. Mrs. Cenic, this is an order, and it is an order that is dated the 17th of June, 1992, Pale, from prime minister Professor Dr. Branko Djeric. And if you look at the item number 1, it is an order to the wartime Presidency and the Executive Board of the municipality of Vogosca to urgently take all necessary steps to make the production of Pretis holding possible. Then if you go down to item number 2 of the English, you'll see "The wartime Presidency is ordered to take all necessary steps to prevent theft." And it goes on, and it concludes in item number 4 that the order is to be carried out immediately and a written report on this is to be sent to the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this is one example, Mrs. Cenic, of orders that were coming from Pale to the authorities in Vogosca to perform certain tasks in Vogosca. Does this in any way refresh your recollection or your testimony, change your testimony in any way as to what you said yesterday, that was that you weren't aware of any such orders?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't change my testimony. I had never seen any instructions issued throughout the time I was there. This document I see here for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have access to documents that were coming from Pale to Mr. Tintor and to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had access to some documents, yes, to the extent that the documents were available to me. As I said, I -- I've seen this particular document for the first time here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So is it your testimony, I take it, Mrs. Cenic, that there were other documents that simply weren't available to you in that period?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I am not aware of any such documents. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn, Mrs. Cenic, next to a topic -- I'm sorry, tab 54.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] 50 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 54. It's at the end of that package. And this is a document that has been previously exhibited as P529, tab 112. And this is a document the Court is familiar with. This is a decision that was issued on the 10th of June by the president of the Presidency, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and it is a Decision on the Establishment of War Commissioners in the Municipalities in Time of Imminent Threat of War or During a State of War. Mrs. Cenic, this is a document that essentially established war commissioners to -- it identified them and ultimately they were identified, I should say, and think came to the municipalities. If you turn to sub-part 3 -- or article 3, you'll see precisely what statutorily they were tasked to do. Article 3 reads a be I'll read just the pertinent parts: "The war commissioners shall maintain the closest possible cooperation with legal authorities. They shall convey directives issued by the War Presidency of the republic." I won't read the rest. So one of the principal functions of the war commissioners was to convey directives. Do you have -- were you aware of that in your conversations? You said you had many conversations with -- with Dr. Koljevic about war commissioners. Were you aware that one of their statutorily mandated functions was to convey directives issued by the War Presidency of the republic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Koljevic did visit Vogosca on one occasion. He spent half a day there, perhaps a bit longer. He also visited the Park Hotel. Professor Koljevic's purpose in being there had to do with commissions. I see this document for the first time, dated the 10th of June, but I can tell you that I met up with Professor Koljevic and spent some time with him. That's to say on the occasion of his visit to Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question was: Were you aware, Mrs. Cenic, that one of the functions of the war commissioners was to convey directives issued by the War Presidency of the republic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't familiar with Article 3, not in its written form. When I arrived at Pale and started working with Professor Koljevic, from that point on I knew that commissioners were supposed to report to the Presidency on the situation in their respective municipalities that they were in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a visit by Dr. Koljevic to Vogosca. Are you aware that other high-level people in the Republika Srpska authorities also visited Vogosca in the period that you were there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, the only person, and I'm talking about the top echelons, was Professor Koljevic. I don't remember anybody else coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, not in your last answer but in the previous one, you said, "I knew," after you started working at Pale, "that commissioners were supposed to report to the Presidency on the position in their respective municipalities." Was this to suggest that they were supposed to but didn't do it, or was there anything of that kind in your answer, or would you say they were supposed to do it and they did it? I mean, my children are opposed to be obedient to their parents. They not always are. You understand what I'm asking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already described the way the four commissioners that we discussed, the way they reported, and in what form their reports were. I never saw a written report. And as I've already told you, I believe that only Dr. Djokanovic submitted something in writing to Professor Koljevic. I did not see any other written reports. Everything was in verbal form, at least when -- when Professor Koljevic's relationship with the Commissioner is concerned. I didn't see any instructions, any document to that effect, I don't know whether anybody listened to those reports or not. I wouldn't dare comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do you know the reason why this was just a report in -- which is not very common in government administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know why reports were not submitted in writing. I can only share with you my opinion about Professor Koljevic. That was his style, and the two of us quite often discussed this matter, and I was of the opinion that there should be something in writing to accompany everything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he give any specific response if you said that -- did you ever express that opinion, is my first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what was his response then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in some segments of our work, he listened to me. I can't say he listened to me because he was my superior. He took my advice is probably a better way to put it. But after a while, he would still resort to his own informal ways, and throughout our work for the three years that was always a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the confidentiality or the sensitivity of the reporting have played any role or was that ever a part of your discussions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not confidentiality that was at stake. If you would allow me to say this. He was just nonchalant in his attitude towards administration and administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As I said, Mrs. Cenic, if you'd turn to tab 34, please. This is an exhibit. It is P65, tab 140. Mrs. Cenic, I'm going to first of all identify the document. This is the minutes from a government meeting of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was held on the 29th of May, 1992, and I would like to direct your attention to page 3 of the English, starting six lines down from the top. You mentioned Mr. Koljevic -- Dr. Koljevic going to Vogosca. Let me read this portion of the document from the government minutes: "It has been concluded that in two days the municipalities of Sarajevo region should be visited. Milan Trbojevic and Velibor Ostojic are responsible for the visits to the municipalities of Vogosca and Ilijas." Now, does this document, accounting for the future visit of Mr. Trbojevic and Mr. Ostojic refresh your recollection at all as to whether persons other than Dr. Koljevic visited the Vogosca municipality while you were there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Milan Trbojevic or Velibor Ostojic's visit. I know both persons very well, and I never saw them in Vogosca. I didn't meet up with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is it possible that they could have paid a visit on the municipality while you were visiting, for example, your parents in Ilidza or you were out of the Hotel Park?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never even heard of their visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back to tab 54 for just a minute.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 54, yes, please. Your evidence yesterday was that -- you were asked a question by my colleague Mr. Stewart whether you had ever heard the term "expanded Presidency." If you look at Article 3, there's a reference to the War Presidency. Do you see that? Do you see that, Mrs. Cenic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you hear of the Presidency referred to as a War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] War Presidency or Presidency, I know the body and I know its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you heard of it referred to both as the Presidency and the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always referred to it as Presidency. This is what it went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to just focus your attention again on another part of your evidence yesterday. You said yesterday in respect of war commissioners, you spent some time on your evidence, and you said that you had attended all of the meetings between the four men who were identified as war commissioners and Dr. Koljevic. That is found at LiveNote 16 -- page 16, line 18, on day 30. During what period of time are you talking about when you say you attended all of the meetings of those commissioners and Dr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment when Professor Koljevic and I started working together, they would come, as I have described. Dragan Djokanovic was almost always on his own, and the other three would sometimes come on their own, sometimes as a group. Sometimes Radovanovic and Poplasen together, sometimes Radovanovic and Jovanovic together. I've described all that, and towards the end of that year --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, my question was, if you can recall, what period are you talking about? Your answer said "from the moment Professor Koljevic and I started working together." Can you put a date on that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Professor Koljevic and I started working to the sometime in October. Towards the end of October, I believe. Again, it's very difficult for me to pinpoint any dates. And these meetings continued until the end of that year and no longer. And why I'm saying that, Professor Koljevic and I shared this small office, and then we moved to a bigger space where he has his own office and I had my office. That's why I remember that those meetings were discontinued after the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to think very carefully, Mrs. Cenic. Are you -- do you recall those meetings to be official meetings of Professor Koljevic and Mr. Poplasen, Dr. Djokanovic, and the others, the other four men, or were those meetings that were, as a result of past contacts with those men, more of a social type of a meeting?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the first part of those meetings, which was rather short, was rather official, and it dealt with the situation in the respective municipalities. And quite a longer bit of those meetings was informal. Those meetings started on a rather formal note but ended in a very informal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand that, and I understood that when you gave your evidence yesterday, Mrs. Cenic, but my question is: What did you understand Professor Koljevic's role to be in respect of the people who were identified as war commissioners?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic was vice-president or, rather, firstly he was a member of the Presidency and that was his task, his duty as a member of the Presidency. He was in charge of talking to the commissioners and working with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your conclusion is based on what when you say that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base my conclusion on Professor Koljevic's words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber has received evidence from the 15th session of the Presidency that the tasks allocated -- task of questions dealing with the war commissioners was allocated to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear it from you now. I know that Professor Koljevic informed me, because we constantly talked, and he informed me that one of his tasks was to cooperate and coordinate the work of the commissioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you -- first of all, in respect of that issue of the war commissioners, Mrs. Cenic, yesterday you testified that Mr. Poplasen was a war commissioner for Ilijas. Let me show you an exhibit. It's extra 2. It's been identified as extra 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If that is could be shown to Mrs. Cenic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar -- has it number already, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour. It's P65, tab 204. And if Mrs. Cenic could also be shown extra 3, which bears the number P65, Treanor tab 205. If you could start with extra 2, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That might not be immediately clear what is extra 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The document that starts -- sorry. The 16 June document that deals with Mr. Jovanovic. And let me just for the record, Mrs. Cenic, identify this document for the record. This is a document from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency dated the 16th of June, 1992. It's a certificate issued by the Presidency, and it appoints -- Professor Dragan Jovanovic is appointed as a state commissioner for the municipality of Ilijas in place of the current commissioner, Jovan Tintor who has been transferred to a new position, and it's signed for the president of the Presidency. If you look at the original B/C/S version, do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This copy is not very legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can't you read the text, or can't you read or recognise the signature only? Ms. Cenic, I asked whether it was -- you said it's not very legible. Is it because of the -- you can't read the signature or that you can't read the typed -- typewritten text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't realise that you were addressing me. I can read the text, the typed-out text, but the signature here is not very legible, and it doesn't speak to me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you worked in Mr. Krajisnik's office for -- you testified for a period of time. This signature, Mrs. Cenic, has been identified in this court and conceded by the Defence to be Mr. Krajisnik's signature.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this first document that speaks about Dragan Jovanovic, I can see just two lines. And as for the second document which mentions Jovo Mijatovic, there is a signature which does look like Mr. Krajisnik's signature. The first signature doesn't look to me like Mr. Krajisnik's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at the meetings with Professor Koljevic and the four individuals you've identified as commissioners, were there any minutes taken of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: These were informal conversations, I take it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not even when they had discussions on the situation in the municipalities. Professor Koljevic wouldn't ask for any minutes to be taken or anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could direct your attention to the document that's dated the 21st of August, 1992. This is a similar document to the previous document that we've seen. It's again the Presidency issuing a certificate, Jovo Mijatovic being appointed as essentially a commissioner for the municipality of Ilidza. Did Mr. Mijatovic ever come and see Dr. Koljevic, Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic did come to see Professor Koljevic. I don't remember him coming in his capacity as a commissioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember conversations with Jovo Mijatovic where he was discussing what was happening in the municipality of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I just want to explore a little bit more your testimony in respect of these commissioners and what you've asserted in this court. If we could turn -- first of all, you've said as far as you know there was nothing in writing that was reported other than perhaps Dr. Djokanovic would occasionally prepare written reports to Dr. Koljevic. Did you ever see any written reports written by Dr. Djokanovic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic who considered himself Professor Koljevic's friend would give information to Dr. Koljevic personally. Those envelopes contained several sheets of paper that Professor Koljevic kept. Those documents were in the form of a private letter. On one occasion I did have an opportunity to see a document of that sort because Professor Koljevic showed them to me, and those documents contained various personal observations and some of which were very personal matters concerning Dr. Djokanovic. Dr. Djokanovic never submitted anything through any official channels, either through me or through somebody else. What I'm saying is, those documents were never officially recorded. They were always delivered personally to Professor Koljevic. Most the meetings between Professor Koljevic and Dr. Djokanovic were held in my absence. If I attended them, it was -- it would be only for a short period of time, and most of the time the two of them spent discussing private and personal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me show you a document. If you'd turn to tab 14, please, Mrs. Cenic. This is Prosecution Exhibit 743.D. Tab 14, Mrs. Cenic, is a document which in the lower left-hand corner is dated June 24, 1992. At the top left-hand corner it's from the Serbian -- Serb municipality of Vogosca, Dr. Nikola Poplasen, republic commissioner, and it's addressed to the Serb republic of BH wartime Presidency. So this document, if you cast an eye on it, Mrs. Then S a written report dealing with the overall situation in the Serb municipality of Vogosca at the moment when Dr. Poplasen was preparing this report. Now, this is one example, Mrs. Cenic, of a written report prepared by wartime commissioners, in this case Dr. Poplasen. And it also touches upon another part of your evidence. And I under stand you only started to work for Dr. Koljevic in October, and in October there were no discussions about prisons. But if you'd turn to sub-part 3 in this document; it says: "Since the prison in Vogosca is illegal in view of our legal regulations, the prison has to be transformed into a subdivision of the correctional facilities in Butnim or" --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mine says "-nim," so thank you for the correction. So, Mrs. Cenic, there were -- strike that. You did know Dr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you saw him when he came to the municipality or --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You never saw him in the Vogosca municipality?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understood your evidence to be yes, but in the last two days that he would come on occasion and then he would leave.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but to Professor Koljevic's office, but not to Vogosca. Please refer to my testimony. I have said very clearly that Mr. Poplasen -- first of all, I never saw Mr. Poplasen in Vogosca. Second of all, I found Mr. Poplasen in the Kikinda building where he slept. Third of all, I said that Mr. Poplasen, like the rest of them, had come there, spent some time there and saw Professor Koljevic and then he would go back. This is the way he did things. The date that is mentioned here, I did not see him in that month, nor do I remember a chance meeting in -- with him in Vogosca, not me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, there is -- Dr. Poplasen has testified in this Chamber, and he has given his evidence that he was in the Vogosca municipality. He gave evidence about this particular document and about the particular facility that he was referring to. So it's again entirely possible that he was there and you just didn't see him. Isn't that right, Mrs. Cenic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite possible. I didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Your Honour. Thank you. Thank you very much, Ms. Cenic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Stewart, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I have no re-examination, Your Honour. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have two questions for you. Yes. You testified about the Presidency and that there were, apart from Presidency meetings, there were broader meetings which you called brain-storming meetings called by Mr. Karadzic. "Brain-storming" suggests that it's just an exchange of views. Is that what you meant by "brain-storming," exchanging views without deciding on matters?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic would often call meetings. He would invite people to ponder, to brain-storm. This was his term, and we took it over from him. And he arrived at the most unexpected times, without any previous announcement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This Chamber has received quite some evidence on meetings where were present Mr. Karadzic, Ms. Plavsic, Professor Koljevic, Mr. Djeric, and Mr. Krajisnik. Minutes of those meetings referring to Presidency, well, there are different descriptions of what the meeting actually was about. In which -- at least it's not represented as an exchange of views but also where decisions are reported to have been taken. I'm trying to find out -- you're talking about Presidency meetings. You're talking about brain-storming meetings. First of all, are you aware of such meetings on a more or less regular basis where the five persons I just mentioned were present, sometimes even one more person or -- how should I understand those meetings? Is that -- in your view, are those Presidency meetings, or are they brain-storming meetings? I can tell you, my problem with calling those Presidency meetings would be that it was not just Mr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, and Professor Koljevic, but regularly Mr. Djeric and Mr. Krajisnik as well. So to that extent, it would not fit into what I understood to be your definition of the Presidency, whereas the decision-taking element in those meetings is not consistent with brain-storming. Could you help me out?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all of us employees, Presidency meant one thing and that was Mr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, and Professor Koljevic. This was Presidency in our view. Everything else was treated as extended collegiums, to use a business term. People would be invited to such meetings without the right to vote. This is a common practice everywhere. For us, the president of the republic was Dr. Karadzic. The vice-presidents were Mrs. Plavsic and Professor Koljevic. And the president of the National Assembly was Mr. Krajisnik. The prime ministers took turns. All these meetings that I referred to by Dr. Karadzic's term were nothing out the ordinary for us. This was just his way. And in our view those were just meetings. What was discussed there I don't know because I never attended those meetings. In any case, this was nothing out of the ordinary, nothing strange. I even believe that Dr. Karadzic often invited some other people from different sides. When I say from different sides, I mean people from various structures who normally would not belong to such meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have received in evidence minutes of those meetings, and as I said, sometimes others were present as well, but the names that appear again and again, sometimes under a heading of Presidency in -- I hope I'm quite correct in -- under an imminent threat of war. We see those two names, Djeric and Krajisnik, appear regularly. So not -- and not described as visitors or -- and usually the meeting is limited to those five persons. So that does not -- your description does not fit entirely into that evidence we received. So I'm asking whether ...

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how to answer your question, what else to say on top of what I've already told you. The evidence that you are commencing is something that I have not seen. I don't have them -- have it. I repeat, in our view the Presidency, the government, the Assembly were bodies that all played their respective roles when they became operational. In my view, President Krajisnik [as interpreted] was president of the assembly, and he remained the president of the municipality until the end of the war and later on. Dr. Karadzic was president of the republic, and I never saw them in any other light, nor do I know of anything else. I also know that everybody liked to talk to Mr. Krajisnik because he was a more stable person than the rest of them. He was even more stable than Professor Koljevic that I worked for. As for those meetings, those of us who worked there treated them the way I described to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there must be a slip at line 14, either by the witness or interpretation, I don't know which, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it it's Mr. Krajisnik was president of the Assembly. And, yes, 14 I have -- on 15 then also and he remain the president of the municipality. That --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've got that on line 14. That's the point, Your Honour, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's clear, and it's undisputed. Let me just -- I'm just checking one thing for a second, if you would allow me time, Ms. Cenic. Yes. I have no further questions on this issue. Then my next question is about the movement of populations. You told us what you discussed about these things and that there was never a plan to remove people, although people finally left the area, just as you did, and, as you said, quite a number of people from other ethnicities did as well. Now, we have heard some evidence on domination, Serb domination in municipalities where the Muslims were in a majority. We have heard some evidence on what goals were mentioned in this period of time, strategic goals. Could you tell me, if you discussed this situation, were you aware that sometimes the Republika Srpska seemed to seek to dominate or at least to be in power in municipalities where there was a non-Serb majority?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know which municipalities you're referring to. In my own view, all the municipalities were disrupted during these conflicts. Nothing was the same. To answer your question specifically, I really don't know of the existence of any plan, nor did I see one anywhere whereby someone was supposed to dominate over someone else in a given part of the country, if there was such thing as domination in Bosnia. After so many years, I can only regret that somebody has deprived me of my life and regret the fact that Cutileiro's plan was rejected, the plan which would have enabled me to live in peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that some territories were claimed by the Republika Srpska where prior to the outbreak of war there was a Serb minority?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me which municipalities you have in mind? I really can't think of the municipalities you might be referring to. I can't even remember the ethnic make-up of individual municipalities. I can speak of the ethnic make-up of the population in Sarajevo, where I grew up, and I knew the place well. The municipality of Tesanj where I worked, was 92 per cent Muslim, today Bosniak. I knew that because I worked there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't learned a -- so if you would give me just one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just take perhaps as an example Vogosca. Was that claimed by the Republika Srpska or not? I'm not quite sure about that, or whether it was just a matter of dividing that municipality. I mean, you said the municipality, no one was there so the Serbs took over, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as the municipality's concerned, I'm referring to the municipal building, the municipal administration building. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I asked you whether there was any -- any administration of the municipality, whether the non-Serbs were involved in any way in the further administration of Vogosca, and I think your answer was no.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now -- now, we have a municipality, and there are examples of other municipalities as well where Serbs claimed to be rulers of that municipality although they are in a minority. How would you expect other parties to respond to such a situation?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Sarajevo was Serb, too, but is no longer. It was Croat, too, but is no longer. We could thus take it municipality by municipality. Every municipality was Bosniak or Muslim, Serb and Croat, each and every one of them, including Tesanj I spoke of, where 92 per cent of the population was Bosniak. At the time I worked there, still there were Croats and Serbs as well. What is absolute and what is relative majority? Who owned more land, who owned more real estate, that's something statistics deals with. That's something that numerous negotiations can testify to. Starting from the Cutileiro's plan, which again I repeat I regret the fact that it was rejected. We would have avoided many things including my visit to this Tribunal. This is the only answer I can give you. There can be no justice in war. We can talk of justice only in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about justice at this moment. I'm not talking about municipalities that -- where no Croats or Bosniaks or Muslims would have lived. I'm talking about municipalities. And I'm not talking about what would have been the preferred solution, because I think that no one would disagree if I would say that a resolution without war was to be preferred under all circumstances. I'm just trying find out -- but let me try to find an example of such a municipality. Perhaps Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a copy of an exhibit which is the -- is the census. Statistics, there are a considerable number of them. Bosanska Krupa, for example, is one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's, for example, take Zvornik. Zvornik was a municipality with an absolute majority of Muslim population. Nevertheless, from what I understand, Zvornik was claimed to become part of Republika Srpska, independent from what Muslims -- whether they would agree with that, being an absolute majority of the population. What would you expect in such a situation the -- to happen? Was that ever discussed among yourselves in terms of movement of population?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We often discussed the movement of population precisely in the sense that no one was left in the place they were supposed to be. We talked about whether there was natural or not. We talked about different parts of the country, the Neretva valley, the Drina valley, the Una valley, the Sana valley. There were quite a few discussions on that topic. We talked about how things should be settled in a way that would be satisfactory for all and whether this was possible at all. Of course, I don't think it fair that I had to leave, but I also don't think it fair that Muslims and Croats had to leave. But to provide you with an explanation as to how this came about, I cannot. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. But -- I do understand that you say it was not fair that I had to leave. It was not fair that Muslims and Croats had to leave. Did you consider -- let's focus just by way of example to Zvornik where these Muslims were in majority and where the Serbs claimed Zvornik to become a part of Republika Srpska. Would you -- if you say "it's unfair that I had to leave," was it considered that the Muslims would have to leave, being the majority, or would you expect that the majority would expect that the Serb minority in that municipality would just -- the Serb minority would just decide that this municipality would be a part of Republika Srpska. Or did you expect, then, the Muslims to leave and say, "Well, you go to the area where -- where you want to live if you don't agree with being in the Republika Srpska," or in the Republic of Serbia in the early stages?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think everyone wanted to be affiliated with their own peoples, to be close to their own peoples to feel better. That's the only answer I can give you. I don't think that Bosnians or Muslims had to accept this or that. They were free to choose what they wanted, just as Serbs were. But of course it was important for everyone to feel safe. And perhaps for that very reason we went too far, and again everyone felt insecure. But, as I said, everyone wanted to be close to their peoples. How far Zvornik is from where the Muslim population is concentrated, how far is Konjic where there were Serbs from the places where Serb population was concentrated. There were migrations, although I have to say I did not see any sort of plan or anything systematic in it. Otherwise, the people would have resorted to what even the representatives of the international community referred to during negotiations as the humane relocation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that, "I don't think that the Bosnians or Muslims had to accept this or that. They were free to choose what they wanted, just as Serbs." Now, I didn't get the impression provisionally from the evidence we heard that the Muslims in Zvornik had chosen to become part of Republika Srpska. Now, if they wanted not to become a part of Republika Srpska, if at the same time the Serbs claimed Zvornik to be or to become part of Republika Srpska, how could those two be reconciled? As you said, they're free to choose. They were in a majority. I never got the impression that they'd chosen that this would be part of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak on their behalf. I can only speak for myself and on behalf of those closest to me that we were hoping for negotiations and a peaceful solution that will let us know what will happen with us. Of course I cannot speak on behalf of Muslims or on behalf of those in Zvornik and say whether they ought to have accepted different solutions or not, because I had never heard of any resettlement plan for Zvornik. I don't -- I don't think that there was one such plan for any part of the country. I don't know what you expect me to say by way of an answer. I thought all of that was provisional until a final solution was found when I would know where to go. There were ongoing negotiations. What was Republika Srpska back then is not what Republika Srpska is today if you look back at 1992, 1993, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not completely the same, but in some respects it is. I'm just wondering whether, and I again take the example of Zvornik, that you expected more or less that people would, I mean, the majority of Muslims would seek place closer to where you said the Muslim population was concentrated. Whether you'd expect them to leave or whether you would expect them -- I mean, what did you have in mind? I'm not asking you what they would decide but how you considered the situation with the majority Muslim population. Nevertheless, municipality claimed by or becoming a part of Republika Srpska not with the explicit consent of the majority of the population.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only answer I can give you is again the same. I don't think they left because there were beds of roses but because they didn't feel secure. They didn't feel safe. Especially this refers to Zvornik which borders with Serbia where in the hinterland there again they had a Serbian population. I did not expect them to accept the Republika Srpska nor did I think that it was fair for the expect the minority to rule over the majority. But there were several cases where the minority ruled over the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you did not consider military control an element for which they may have left? I mean, military control by the Serbs. And just to give you a few more examples, for example, Vlasenica or Sanski Most, all municipalities in which the Serbs why in a minority, but at a certain moment gained military control over if not all then most of the territory of those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were probably such days of case cases on the other side too, not just on this side. And, as I said, if I may be allowed to finish, that is why I said that I did not think that they left because things were rosy but because they felt the presence of the army. They had their backs to Serbia and they felt threatened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I then understand your answer well if you say just as happened in what is now the situation in those parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina not being Republika Srpska, similarly the Muslims under the situation which was a situation of military control by the other party, yesterday I think you agreed with me that it would be intimidation as well, that they felt threatened under those circumstances and felt, just as you felt, that you had no choice but to leave, that they would be in a similar situation.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similar situations existed on all sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was this something, just in general terms, if you gained military control over a certain area, if in circumstances there was intimidation, as you experienced yourself, would you consider it a normal or expectable -- expected cause of events that people would leave? I mean, the threatened population, whether minority or majority, but those who had no military control.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the stronger side, as you put it, or the armed side was of the other ethnicity, then members of different ethnicities left. For instance, if those were Serbs, then the Muslims would leave. We had stories from World War II that were fresh in people's memories. For instance, my parents still remembered those stories, and they instilled them with fear, which was quite natural, for that matter. We had not cured or remedied the causes of that earlier war and had already found ourselves with our hands full of this new war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the matters I just discussed with you because I asked for your opinion on what you would expect, were these matters of -- well, portions, substantial portions of the population moving out, at least the possibility of them moving out, was that ever part of the discussion on population movement, as you told us that you -- that population movement was included in your conversations.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the conversations which had to do with this topic were the ones I had with Professor Koljevic. I have to tell you right away that Professor Koljevic was in favour of negotiations, persistent negotiations in order to find a definite solution that would be satisfactory for the population, to find such a solution that would provide safety for all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. Any questions arising from the Bench's questions? Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I need to come over here to look at the transcript. Mrs. Cenic, your answer to one of Judge Orie's questions was, which is found at page 64, line 18 to 20, you said, "I also know that everybody liked to talk to Mr. Krajisnik because he was a more stable person than the rest of them. He was even more stable than Professor Koljevic that I worked for." Now, you have told us, Mrs. Cenic, that in respect of the way in which Professor Koljevic worked, he didn't take minutes at meetings, he didn't record meetings, for example, of meetings with the war commissioners that you personally attended. How would you describe Mr. Krajisnik's manner of approaching the same problem, that is the attendance of meetings and the recording of what happened in them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How does this arise out of the questions, Your Honour? Both Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik are mentioned, but it's a completely different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, I do agree with Mr. Stewart that how Mr. Koljevic took notes at the meetings does not open the gate for asking to whoever else recorded what was discussed at such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, her answer invited a question insofar as she said, "He was a more stable person than the rest of them, and he was more stable than Professor Koljevic, who I worked for." And so I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the two are not -- not really related. Taking notes and stability are two different matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, if I may, Your Honour, I'd ask leave of the Court to have that question answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No. The Chamber decides that you'll not -- that the question be answered. Any other question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No other questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your testimony in this court, Mrs. Cenic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered many questions, a couple of days here, questions both from the Defence, Prosecution, and the Bench. I'd like to thank you very much, and I'm at least happy that we could conclude today, because I understood that it would have caused you considerable problems if we would not have been able to do so. So I'd like to thank you very much, and then I wish you safe trip home again so that you can continue your work on Monday, as you wished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The difficulty lies in the fact that students can't wait, and I don't have a substitute to stand in for me, and that's why I thank you for finishing today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. We will adjourn until next Monday at quarter past two in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
